docs.title: Welcome to Froom
docs.text:
Froom provides a neat SQLite abstraction for your Flutter applications inspired by the Room persistence library. It comes with automatic mapping between in-memory objects and database rows while still offering full control of the database with the use of SQL. As a consequence, it's necessary to have an understanding of SQL and SQLite in order to harvest Froom's full potential.

  • null-safe
  • typesafe
  • reactive
  • lightweight
  • SQL centric
  • no hidden magic
  • no hidden costs
  • iOS, Android, Linux, macOS, Windows, web

Important

The library is open to contributions! Refer to GitHub Discussions for questions, ideas, and discussions.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The components for storing and accessing data are Entity, Data Access Object (DAO) and Database.

The first, Entity, represents a persistent class and thus a database table. DAOs manage the access to Entities and take care of the mapping between in-memory objects and table rows. Lastly, Database, is the central access point to the underlying SQLite database. It holds the DAOs and, beyond that, takes care of initializing the database and its schema. Room serves as the source of inspiration for this composition, because it allows creating a clean separation of the component's responsibilities.

The figure shows the relationship between Entity, DAO and Database.

docs.title: Data Access Objects
docs.text:
These components are responsible for managing access to the underlying SQLite database and are defined as abstract classes with method signatures and query statements. DAO classes can use inherited methods by implementing and extending classes while also using mixins.

@dao
abstract class PersonDao {
  @Query('SELECT * FROM Person')
  Future<List<Person>> findAllPeople();

  @Query('SELECT * FROM Person WHERE id = :id')
  Stream<Person?> findPersonById(int id);

  @insert
  Future<void> insertPerson(Person person);
}

docs.title: Queries
docs.text:
Method signatures turn into query methods by adding the @Query() annotation with the query in parenthesis to them. Be mindful about the correctness of your SQL statements as they are only partly validated while generating the code. These queries have to return either a Future or a Stream of an entity, Dart core type or void. Retrieval of Dart Core types such as String, double, int, double, Uint8List can be used if you want to get all records from a certain column or return COUNT records in the table. Returning Future<void> comes in handy whenever you want to delete the full content of a table, for instance. Some query method examples can be seen in the following.

A function returning a single item will return null when no matching row is found. Thereby, the function is required to return a nullable type. For example Person?. This way, we leave the handling of an absent row up to you and don't attempt to guess intention.

@Query('SELECT * FROM Person WHERE id = :id')
Future<Person?> findPersonById(int id);

@Query('SELECT * FROM Person WHERE id = :id AND name = :name')
Future<Person?> findPersonByIdAndName(int id, String name);

@Query('SELECT COUNT(id) FROM Person')
Future<int?> getPeopleCount(); // fetch records count

@Query('SELECT name FROM Person')
Future<List<String>> getAllPeopleNames(); // fetch all records from one column

@Query('SELECT * FROM Person')
Future<List<Person>> findAllPeople(); // select multiple items

@Query('SELECT * FROM Person')
Stream<List<Person>> findAllPeopleAsStream(); // stream return

@Query('DELETE FROM Person')
Future<void> deleteAllPeople(); // query without returning an entity

@Query('SELECT * FROM Person WHERE id IN (:ids)')
Future<List<Person>> findPeopleWithIds(List<int> ids); // query with IN clause

@Query('SELECT * FROM Person WHERE nickname IS :nickname')
Future<List<Person>> findPeopleWithNickname(String? nickname); // nullable parameters are bound as NULL

@Query('SELECT * FROM Person LIMIT :count OFFSET :offset')
Future<List<Person>> findPeople({int offset = 0, required int count}); // optional and named parameters

Nullable parameters are bound as NULL. As = NULL is never true in SQL, compare them with IS to match NULL values. List parameters have to be non-nullable and referenced in parentheses, either with IN (:list) or as a row value, e.g. (name, id) > (:keySet) with a List<Object> for values of different types.

Query arguments, when using SQLite's LIKE operator, have to be supplied by the input of a method. It's not possible to define a pattern matching argument like %foo% in the query itself.

// dao
@Query('SELECT * FROM Person WHERE name LIKE :name')
Future<List<Person>> findPeopleWithNamesLike(String name);

// usage
final name = '%foo%';
await dao.findPeopleWithNamesLike(name);

docs.title: Data Changes
docs.text: Use the @insert, @update, @upsert and @delete annotations for inserting and changing persistent data. All these methods accept single or multiple entity instances.

docs.title: Insert
docs.text:
@insert marks a method as an insertion method. When using the capitalized @Insert you can specify a conflict strategy. Else it just defaults to aborting the insert. These methods can return a Future of either void, int or List<int>. - void return nothing - int return primary key of inserted item - List<int> return primary keys of inserted items

@Insert(onConflict: OnConflictStrategy.rollback)
Future<void> insertPerson(Person person);

@insert
Future<List<int>> insertPeople(List<Person> people);

docs.title: Update
docs.text:
@update marks a method as an update method. When using the capitalized @Update you can specify a conflict strategy. Else it just defaults to aborting the update. These methods can return a Future of either void or int. - void return nothing - int return number of changed rows

@Update(onConflict: OnConflictStrategy.replace)
Future<void> updatePerson(Person person);

@update
Future<int> updatePeople(List<Person> people);

docs.title: Upsert
docs.text:
@upsert marks a method as an upsert method, just like Room's @Upsert. It first tries to insert the entity. When the insertion fails because of a unique constraint conflict (e.g. the primary key already exists), the existing row is updated instead. If no row with the primary key exists, e.g. because the conflict was caused by another unique index, the original exception is rethrown instead of silently dropping the item. Unlike @Insert(onConflict: OnConflictStrategy.replace), the existing row is not deleted, so foreign key ON DELETE actions (e.g. cascading deletes) are not triggered. Each upsert method runs in a single transaction. Upsert methods returning void use a single batch of native INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE statements when SQLite supports them (version 3.24.0 and above, except for virtual tables like FTS tables), which is considerably faster for large lists and behaves the same. As virtual tables like FTS tables don't enforce unique primary keys, their entities are updated by primary key first and only inserted when no row got updated. These methods can return a Future of either void, int or List<int>. - void return nothing - int return primary key of inserted item or -1 if the item got updated (single item parameter only) - List<int> return primary keys of inserted items or -1 for updated items (single list parameter only)

@upsert
Future<void> upsertPerson(Person person);

@upsert
Future<List<int>> upsertPeople(List<Person> people);

Upsert methods can take multiple parameters, each being an entity or a list of entities. All of them are upserted in the same transaction, so a failure rolls back every parameter. Such methods have to return Future<void>.

@upsert
Future<void> upsertPublisherAndBooks(Publisher publisher, List<Book> books);

When specifying a target entity, the parameters can be partial entities. A partial entity is a class containing a subset of the columns of the target entity, matched by column name. Only its columns are inserted or updated, the other columns keep their values or defaults. It has to contain the primary key columns, unless the primary key is auto generated, and all non-nullable columns of the target entity. Fields of non-nullable columns have to be non-nullable as well. Fields need the same type as their column and use the type converters of the target entity.

class BookTitle {
  final int id;

  final String title;

  BookTitle(this.id, this.title);
}

@Upsert(entity: Book)
Future<void> upsertBookTitle(BookTitle bookTitle);

docs.title: Delete
docs.text:
@delete marks a method as a deletion method. These methods can return a Future of either void or int. - void return nothing - int return number of deleted rows

@delete
Future<void> deletePerson(Person person);

@delete
Future<int> deletePeople(List<Person> people);

docs.title: Streams
docs.text:
As already mentioned, queries cannot only return values once when called but also continuous streams of query results. The returned streams keep you in sync with the changes happening in the database tables. This feature plays well with the StreamBuilder widget which accepts a stream of values and rebuilds itself whenever there is a new emission. These methods return broadcast streams and thus, can have multiple listeners.

A function returning a stream of single items will emit null when no matching row is found. Thereby, it's necessary to make the function return a stream of a nullable type. For example Stream<Person?>. In case you're not interested in nulls, you can simply use Stream.where((value) => value != null) to get rid of them.

// definition
@dao
abstract class PersonDao {
  @Query('SELECT * FROM Person WHERE id = :id')
  Stream<Person?> findPersonByIdAsStream(int id);

  @Query('SELECT * FROM Person')
  Stream<List<Person>> findAllPeopleAsStream();
}

// usage
StreamBuilder<List<Person>>(
  stream: dao.findAllPeopleAsStream(),
  builder: (BuildContext context, AsyncSnapshot<List<Person>> snapshot) {
    // do something with the values here
  },
);

Attention

  • Methods annotated with @insert, @update, @upsert and @delete trigger Stream emissions, as well as INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE statements of @Query() methods, which notify the streams of the changed table.
  • It is now possible to return a Stream if the function queries a database view. But it will fire on any @update, @insert, @upsert, @delete events in the whole database, which can get quite taxing on the runtime. Please add it only if you know what you are doing! This is mostly due to the complexity of detecting which entities are involved in a database view.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
Whenever you want to perform some operations in a transaction you have to add the @transaction annotation to the method. It's also required to add the async modifier. These methods have to return a Future.

@transaction
Future<void> replacePeople(List<Person> people) async {
  await deleteAllPeople();
  await insertPeople(people);
}

docs.title: Inheritance
docs.text:
Data access object classes support inheritance as shown in the following. There is no limit to inheritance levels and thus, each abstract parent can have another abstract parent. Bear in mind that only abstract classes allow method signatures without an implementation body and thereby, make sure to position your to-be-inherited methods in an abstract class and extend this class with your DAO.

@dao
abstract class PersonDao extends AbstractDao<Person> {
  @Query('SELECT * FROM Person WHERE id = :id')
  Future<Person?> findPersonById(int id);
}

abstract class AbstractDao<T> {
  @insert
  Future<void> insertItem(T item);
}

// usage
final person = Person(1, 'Simon');
await personDao.insertItem(person);

final result = await personDao.findPersonById(1);

docs.title: Database Views
docs.text:
If you want to define static SELECT-statements which return different types than your entities, your best option is to use @DatabaseView. A database view can be understood as a virtual table, which can be queried like a real table.

A database view in froom is defined and used similarly to entities, with the main difference being that access is read-only, which means that update, insert, upsert and delete functions are not possible. Similarly to entities, the class name is used if no viewName was set.

@DatabaseView('SELECT distinct(name) AS name FROM person', viewName: 'name')
class Name {
  final String name;

  Name(this.name);
}

Database views do not have any foreign/primary keys or indices. Instead, you should manually define indices which fit to your statement and put them into the @Entity annotation of the involved entities.

Setters, getters and static fields are automatically ignored (like in entities), you can specify additional fields to ignore by annotating them with @ignore.

After defining a database view in your code, you have to add it to your database by adding it to the views field of the @Database annotation:

@Database(version: 1, entities: [Person], views: [Name])
abstract class AppDatabase extends FroomDatabase {
  // DAO getters
}

You can then query the view via a DAO function like an entity.

It is possible for DatabaseViews to inherit common fields from a base class, just like in entities.

When upgrading the database with migrations, the views of the database are recreated with their current queries after the migrations, as views don't hold any data. Thus, changing the query of a view only requires a database version increase with a migration, which doesn't have to touch the view.

Attention

It is now possible to return a Stream object from a DAO method which queries a database view. But it will fire on any @update, @insert, @upsert, @delete events in the whole database, which can get quite taxing on the runtime. Please add it only if you know what you are doing! This is mostly due to the complexity of detecting which entities are involved in a database view.

docs.title: Entities
docs.text:
An entity is a persistent class. Froom automatically creates the mappings between the in-memory objects and database table rows. It's possible to supply custom metadata to Froom by adding optional values to the Entity annotation. It has the additional attribute of tableName which opens up the possibility to use a custom name for that specific entity instead of using the class name. foreignKeys allows adding foreign keys to the entity. More information on how to use these can be found in the Foreign Keys section. Indices are supported as well. They can be used by adding an Index to the indices value of the entity. For further information of these, please refer to the Indices section.

@PrimaryKey marks property of a class as the primary key column. This property has to be of type int. The value can be automatically generated by SQLite when autoGenerate is enabled. To let SQLite generate the key when inserting, set a nullable key to null, or, like in Room, a non-nullable int key to 0. For more information about primary keys and especially compound primary keys, refer to the Primary Keys section.

@ColumnInfo enables custom mapping of single table columns. With the annotation it's possible to give columns a custom name. defaultValue adds an SQL default value to the column, which is used when a row is inserted without a value for it, e.g. by a @Query INSERT statement or a partial entity of @Upsert. Like in Room, text values are quoted automatically, except for SQLite constants like NULL or CURRENT_TIMESTAMP and expressions in parentheses, e.g. @ColumnInfo(defaultValue: 'Guest') or @ColumnInfo(defaultValue: '0'). Inserting an entity always uses its field values. When adding such a column in a migration, declare the default value in the ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT ... statement as well. If you want a table's column to be nullable, mark the entity's field as nullable. More information can be found in the Null Safety section.

Attention

  • Froom uses the unnamed constructor of the entity class for creating in-memory objects from database rows. Without an unnamed constructor, the first public named constructor is used.
  • There needs to be a constructor.
  • Fields which aren't initialized by the constructor are assigned via their setters, so entities can also use a constructor without parameters and mutable fields.
  • Fields of superclasses and mixins are columns of the entity as well, e.g. when applying EquatableMixin.
@Entity(tableName: 'person')
class Person {
  @PrimaryKey(autoGenerate: true)
  final int id;

  @ColumnInfo(name: 'custom_name')
  final String name;

  Person(this.id, this.name);
}

docs.title: Supported Types
docs.text:
Froom entities can hold values of the following Dart types which map to their corresponding SQLite types and vice versa.

  • int - INTEGER
  • double - REAL
  • String - TEXT
  • bool - INTEGER (0 = false, 1 = true)
  • Uint8List - BLOB
  • enum - INTEGER (records by the index 0..n)

In case you want to store sophisticated Dart objects that can be represented by one of the above types, take a look at Type Converters.

docs.title: Primary Keys
docs.text:
Whenever a compound primary key is required (e.g. n-m relationships), the syntax for setting the keys differs from the previously mentioned way of setting primary keys. Instead of annotating a field with @PrimaryKey, the @Entity annotation's primaryKey attribute is used. It accepts a list of column names that make up the compound primary key.

@Entity(primaryKeys: ['id', 'name'])
class Person {
  final int id;

  final String name;

  Person(this.id, this.name);
}

docs.title: Foreign Keys
docs.text:
Add a list of ForeignKeys to the Entity annotation of the referencing entity. childColumns define the columns of the current entity, whereas parentColumns define the columns of the parent entity. Foreign key actions can get triggered after defining them for the onUpdate and onDelete properties.

@Entity(
  tableName: 'dog',
  foreignKeys: [
    ForeignKey(
      childColumns: ['owner_id'],
      parentColumns: ['id'],
      entity: Person,
    )
  ],
)
class Dog {
  @PrimaryKey()
  final int id;

  final String name;

  @ColumnInfo(name: 'owner_id')
  final int ownerId;

  Dog(this.id, this.name, this.ownerId);
}

docs.title: Indices
docs.text:
Indices help speeding up query, join and grouping operations. For more information on SQLite indices please refer to the official documentation. To create an index with froom, add a list of indices to the @Entity annotation. The example below shows how to create an index on the custom_name column of the entity.

The index, moreover, can be named by using its name attribute. To set an index to be unique, use the unique attribute. 

@Entity(tableName: 'person', indices: [Index(value: ['custom_name'])])
class Person {
  @primaryKey
  final int id;

  @ColumnInfo(name: 'custom_name')
  final String name;

  Person(this.id, this.name);
}

A partial index only includes the rows for which its where expression is true. This allows e.g. a unique index which permits multiple rows without a value.

@Entity(indices: [
  Index(value: ['email'], unique: true, where: 'email IS NOT NULL'),
])
class Account {
  @primaryKey
  final int id;

  final String? email;

  Account(this.id, this.email);
}

Besides column names, an index can contain expressions. Any value which isn't a column name of the entity is used as an expression, e.g. a case-insensitive unique index on email:

@Entity(indices: [
  Index(value: ['lower(email)'], unique: true),
])

docs.title: Full Text Search
docs.text:
Like Room's @Fts3 and @Fts4, annotating an entity with @fts3/@Fts3() or @fts4/@Fts4() stores it in an SQLite FTS virtual table, which supports fast full text search with the MATCH operator. The tokenizer, e.g. FtsTokenizer.unicode61 for non-ASCII text, and its arguments can be set with the tokenizer and tokenizerArgs attributes.

FTS entities need a primary key like other entities, which is commonly mapped to a column named rowid, as shown below.

@Entity(tableName: 'mail')
@Fts4(tokenizer: FtsTokenizer.unicode61)
class Mail {
  @PrimaryKey()
  @ColumnInfo(name: 'rowid')
  final int id;

  final String text;

  Mail(this.id, this.text);
}

@dao
abstract class MailDao {
  @Query('SELECT * FROM mail WHERE text MATCH :query')
  Future<List<Mail>> findMails(String query);

  @insert
  Future<void> insertMail(Mail mail);
}

// usage
await mailDao.findMails('flutter'); // contains the word "flutter"
await mailDao.findMails('flut*'); // contains a word starting with "flut"

Attention

  • FTS tables don't enforce constraints like unique primary keys or foreign keys, and index all columns. Inserting an existing primary key adds another row, use @upsert to update existing rows instead.
  • Indices and type affinities don't apply to FTS tables, so better keep searchable text in FTS entities and other data in regular entities.
  • The SQLite builds bundled by sqlite3, which the default database factory uses, don't support FTS3 and FTS4, see Platform Support. Use FTS5 instead.

docs.title: FTS5
docs.text:
Unlike Room, Froom supports FTS5 tables with @fts5/@Fts5(), which all SQLite builds bundled by sqlite3 support, including the encrypted ones. The SQLite of Android, which the sqflite plugin uses, lacks FTS5, so pass the FFI database factory to the builder for FTS5 entities on Android, see Platform Support. Besides tokenizer (FtsTokenizer.unicode61 by default, or ascii, porter and trigram) and tokenizerArgs, @Fts5() takes the lengths of prefixes to index for faster prefix queries, and the columns which are stored but notIndexed.

The primary key of FTS5 entities has to be an integer field of the column rowid, which is the row id of the table. As FTS5 tables don't return their row id for *, queries have to select it explicitly.

@Entity(tableName: 'note')
@Fts5(prefixes: [2, 3], notIndexed: ['author'])
class Note {
  @PrimaryKey(autoGenerate: true)
  @ColumnInfo(name: 'rowid')
  final int id;

  final String text;

  final String author;

  Note(this.id, this.text, this.author);
}

@dao
abstract class NoteDao {
  @Query('SELECT rowid, * FROM note WHERE note MATCH :query')
  Future<List<Note>> findNotes(String query);
}

Unlike FTS3 and FTS4 tables, FTS5 tables enforce unique row ids, and their entities can't have indices or foreign keys.

docs.title: Ignoring Fields
docs.text:
Getters, setters and all static fields of entities are ignored by default and thus excluded from the library's mapping. In case further fields should be ignored, the @ignore annotation should be used and applied as shown in the following snippet.

class Person {
  @primaryKey
  final int id;

  final String name;

  @ignore
  String nickname;

  // ignored by default
  String get combinedName => "$name ($nickname)";

  Person(this.id, this.name);
}

docs.title: Inheritance
docs.text:
Just like Daos, entities (and database views) can inherit from a common base class and use their fields. The entity just has to extend the base class. This construct will be treated as if all the fields in the base class are part of the entity, meaning the database table will have all columns of the entity and the base class.

The base class does not have to have a separate annotation for the class. Its fields can be annotated just like normal entity columns. Foreign keys and indices have to be declared in the entity and can't be defined in the base class.

class BaseObject {
  @PrimaryKey()
  final int id;

  @ColumnInfo(name: 'create_time')
  final String createTime;

  @ColumnInfo(name: 'update_time')
  final String updateTime;

  BaseObject(
    this.id,
    this.updateTime, {
    String createTime,
  }) : this.createTime = createTime ?? DateTime.now().toString();

  @override
  List<Object> get props => [];
}

@Entity(tableName: 'comments')
class Comment extends BaseObject {
  final String author;

  final String content;

  Comment(
    this.author, {
    int id,
    this.content = '', 
    String createTime,
    String updateTime,
  }) : super(id, updateTime, createTime: createTime);
}

docs.title: Migrating from Floor
docs.text:
If you're migrating from Floor to Froom, see our Migration Guide for detailed instructions and an automated migration script.

⚠️ Important: Always backup your project before migration!

docs.title: 1. Setup Dependencies
docs.text:
Add the runtime dependency froom as well as the generator froom_generator to your pubspec.yaml. The third dependency is build_runner which has to be included as a dev dependency just like the generator.

  • froom holds all the code you are going to use in your application.
  • froom_generator includes the code for generating the database classes.
  • build_runner enables a concrete way of generating source code files.
dependencies:
  flutter:
    sdk: flutter
  froom: ^x.x.x

dev_dependencies:
  froom_generator: ^x.x.x
  build_runner: ^x.x.x

💡 Tip: Use command for easier installation: 

dart pub add froom dev:froom_generator dev:build_runner

docs.title: 2. Create an Entity
docs.text:
It will represent a database table as well as the scaffold of your business object. @entity marks the class as a persistent class. It's required to add a primary key to your table. You can do so by adding the @primaryKey annotation to an int property. There is no restriction on where you put the file containing the entity.

// entity/person.dart

import 'package:froom/froom.dart';

@entity
class Person {
  @primaryKey
  final int id;

  final String name;

  Person(this.id, this.name);
}

docs.title: 3. Create a DAO (Data Access Object)
docs.text:
This component is responsible for managing access to the underlying SQLite database. The abstract class contains the method signatures for querying the database which have to return a Future or Stream.

  • You can define queries by adding the @Query annotation to a method. The SQL statement has to get added in parenthesis. The method must return a Future or Stream of the Entity you're querying for.
  • @insert marks a method as an insertion method.
  • @upsert marks a method as an upsert method, which inserts an entity or updates it if it already exists. See Upsert.
// dao/person_dao.dart

import 'package:froom/froom.dart';

import '../entity/person.dart';

@dao
abstract class PersonDao {
  @Query('SELECT * FROM Person')
  Future<List<Person>> findAllPersons();

  @Query('SELECT * FROM Person WHERE id = :id')
  Stream<Person?> findPersonById(int id);

  @insert
  Future<void> insertPerson(Person person);
}

docs.title: 4. Create the Database
docs.text:
It has to be an abstract class which extends FroomDatabase. Furthermore, it's required to add @Database() to the signature of the class. Make sure to add the created entity to the entities attribute of the @Database annotation. In order to make the generated code work, it's required to also add the listed imports.

Make sure to add part 'database.g.dart'; beneath the imports of this file. It's important to note that 'database' has to get exchanged with the filename of the database definition. In this case, the file is named database.dart.

// database.dart

// required package imports
import 'dart:async';
import 'package:froom/froom.dart';
import 'package:froom/sqflite.dart' as sqflite;

import 'dao/person_dao.dart';
import 'entity/person.dart';

part 'database.g.dart'; // the generated code will be there

@Database(version: 1, entities: [Person])
abstract class AppDatabase extends FroomDatabase {
  PersonDao get personDao;
}

docs.title: 5. Run the Code Generator
docs.text: Run the generator with dart run build_runner build. To automatically run it, whenever a file changes, use dart run build_runner watch.

docs.title: 6. Use the Generated Code
docs.text:
For obtaining an instance of the database, use the generated $FroomAppDatabase class, which allows access to a database builder. The name is being composed by $Froom and the database class name. The string passed to databaseBuilder() will be the database file name, which is placed in the default databases directory of the platform. To store the database somewhere else, pass an absolute path instead, e.g. one based on getApplicationSupportDirectory() of the path_provider package. Make sure that its directory exists. For initializing the database, call build() and make sure to await the result.

In order to retrieve the PersonDao instance, invoking the persoDao getter on the database instance is enough. Its functions can be used as shown in the following snippet.

final database = await $FroomAppDatabase.databaseBuilder('app_database.db').build();

final personDao = database.personDao;
final person = Person(1, 'Frank');

await personDao.insertPerson(person);
final result = await personDao.findPersonById(1);

To delete all data while keeping the database schema, e.g. when a user logs out, call clearAllTables() on the database. It deletes the rows of all entity tables in a single transaction, resets the AUTOINCREMENT counters and notifies the streams of all entities.

await database.clearAllTables();

On Android and iOS, add the sqflite plugin to use the SQLite of the system, like Floor. For the web, and for choosing the SQLite library or encrypting the database, see Platform Support.

For further examples take a look at the example and test directories.

docs.title: In Memory Database
docs.text:
To instantiate an in-memory database, use the static inMemoryDatabaseBuilder() method of the generated $FroomAppDatabase class instead of databaseBuilder().

final database = await $FroomAppDatabase.inMemoryDatabaseBuilder().build();

In-memory databases are not stored, so they aren't encrypted with a password of their builder.

docs.title: Initialization Callback
docs.text:
In order to hook into Froom's database initialization process, Callback should be used. It allows the invocation of three separate callbacks which are triggered when the database has been

  • initialized for the first time (onCreate).
  • opened (onOpen).
  • upgraded (onUpgrade).

Each callback is optional.

Their usage can be seen in the following snippet.

final callback = Callback(
   onCreate: (database, version) { /* database has been created */ },
   onOpen: (database) { /* database has been opened */ },
   onUpgrade: (database, startVersion, endVersion) { /* database has been upgraded */ },
);

final database = await $FroomAppDatabase
    .databaseBuilder('app_database.db')
    .addCallback(callback)
    .build();

docs.title: Isolates
docs.text:
Froom accesses SQLite through a sqflite DatabaseFactory, which determines where the queries run:

  • The sqflite plugin, the default on Android and iOS for apps depending on sqflite, runs them on a native background thread.
  • The FFI factory databaseFactoryFfi, the default on the other native platforms, runs them on a background isolate. Pass databaseFactoryFfiNoIsolate to databaseFactory() of the database builder to run them on the current isolate instead.
  • On the web, they run in a shared worker.

Changes are only reported to the streams of the database instance that made them. Writes of other isolates, processes or browser tabs to the same database don't update the streams.

You can do some further reading on sqflite's background work mechanisms here.

docs.title: Migration from Floor to Froom
docs.text: This guide will help you migrate your existing Floor project to Froom. Froom is built as a modern replacement for Floor, offering better compatibility with current Flutter versions and additional features.

docs.title: Version Compatibility
docs.text:
Before migrating, ensure you're using the correct Froom version based on your dependencies:

source_gen Version Froom Version 3.x.x and above 3.x.x 2.x.x 2.0.4

docs.title: ⚠️ Important: Backup Your Project
docs.text:
Before starting the migration, always create a complete backup of your project!

You can create a backup by: 

# Create a backup directory
cp -r your_project_directory your_project_directory_backup

# Or use git to commit your current state
git add .
git commit -m "Backup before Floor to Froom migration"

The automated migration script will also create a backup automatically, but it's always safer to have your own backup.

docs.title: Migration Steps
docs.text: 💡 Recommended: Use our automated migration scripts to handle the migration process automatically. The manual steps below are for reference or custom migration needs.

docs.title: 1. Update Dependencies
docs.text:
Replace Floor dependencies with Froom in your pubspec.yaml:

Before (Floor): 

dependencies:
  floor: ^1.4.2

dev_dependencies:
  floor_generator: ^1.4.2
  build_runner: ^2.1.2

After (Froom): 

dependencies:
  froom: ^x.x.x

dev_dependencies:
  froom_generator: ^x.x.x
  build_runner: ^x.x.x

💡 Tip: Use command for easier installation: 

dart pub add froom dev:froom_generator dev:build_runner
This command automatically adds the latest compatible versions without manually editing pubspec.yaml.

docs.title: 2. Update Import Statements
docs.text:
Replace all Floor package imports with Froom imports:

Before: 

import 'package:floor/floor.dart';
import 'package:floor_annotation/floor_annotation.dart';

After: 

import 'package:froom/froom.dart';
import 'package:froom_annotation/froom_annotation.dart';

docs.title: 3. Update Database Class
docs.text:
Update your database class to extend FroomDatabase instead of FloorDatabase:

Before: 

@Database(version: 1, entities: [Person])
abstract class AppDatabase extends FloorDatabase {
  PersonDao get personDao;
}

After: 

@Database(version: 1, entities: [Person])
abstract class AppDatabase extends FroomDatabase {
  PersonDao get personDao;
}

docs.title: 4. Update Database Builder
docs.text:
Update the database builder class name:

Before: 

final database = await $FloorAppDatabase.databaseBuilder('app_database.db').build();

After: 

final database = await $FroomAppDatabase.databaseBuilder('app_database.db').build();

docs.title: 5. Regenerate Code
docs.text:
After making these changes, regenerate your database code:

flutter packages pub run build_runner clean
flutter packages pub run build_runner build

docs.title: Automated Migration Scripts
docs.text:
We provide migration scripts for different platforms to automate most of the migration process:

📁 Script Location: All migration scripts can be found in the scripts directory of this repository.

docs.title: Linux/macOS (Bash)
docs.text:
# Make script executable
chmod +x scripts/migrate_floor_to_froom.sh

# Interactive mode (default) - asks before creating backup
./scripts/migrate_floor_to_froom.sh

# Force create backup without asking
./scripts/migrate_floor_to_froom.sh --backup

# Skip all confirmations (no backup)
./scripts/migrate_floor_to_froom.sh --yes

# Create backup and skip confirmations
./scripts/migrate_floor_to_froom.sh --backup --yes

# Specify project path (multiple ways)
./scripts/migrate_floor_to_froom.sh /path/to/project              # Positional argument
./scripts/migrate_floor_to_froom.sh --path /path/to/project       # Named option
./scripts/migrate_floor_to_froom.sh -p /path/to/project           # Short option

# Combined options
./scripts/migrate_floor_to_froom.sh --path /path/to/project --backup --yes

# Show help
./scripts/migrate_floor_to_froom.sh --help

docs.title: Windows (PowerShell)
docs.text:
⚠️ PowerShell Execution Policy Notice:

Windows PowerShell may restrict script execution due to security policies. If you encounter execution policy errors, you have several options:

Option 1: Use the batch launcher (Recommended for most users) 

# This automatically handles execution policy issues
.\scripts\run_migration.bat

Option 2: Temporarily bypass execution policy 

# Run migration with bypassed policy (one-time)
PowerShell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File ".\scripts\migrate_floor_to_froom.ps1"

Option 3: Change execution policy (Requires Administrator) 

# Open PowerShell as Administrator and run:
Set-ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser

# Or for system-wide (requires elevated permissions):
Set-ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Force

Option 4: Unrestricted execution (Less secure, not recommended) 

# Temporarily allow all scripts (use with caution)
Set-ExecutionPolicy Unrestricted -Scope CurrentUser

# Remember to revert after migration:
Set-ExecutionPolicy Restricted -Scope CurrentUser

Regular Usage (after policy is configured): 

# Interactive mode (default) - asks before creating backup
.\scripts\migrate_floor_to_froom.ps1

# Force create backup without asking
.\scripts\migrate_floor_to_froom.ps1 -Backup

# Skip all confirmations (no backup)
.\scripts\migrate_floor_to_froom.ps1 -Yes

# Create backup and skip confirmations
.\scripts\migrate_floor_to_froom.ps1 -Backup -Yes

# Specify project path
.\scripts\migrate_floor_to_froom.ps1 -Path "C:\path\to\project"

# Combined options
.\scripts\migrate_floor_to_froom.ps1 -Path "C:\path\to\project" -Backup -Yes

# Show help
.\scripts\migrate_floor_to_froom.ps1 -Help

docs.title: Windows (Batch Launcher)
docs.text:
For Windows users who may have PowerShell execution policy restrictions:

# GUI launcher that handles PowerShell execution policy automatically
.\scripts\run_migration.bat

The batch launcher will: - Check PowerShell execution policy - Offer to bypass or change policy if needed - Provide an interactive menu to select migration scripts - Handle script arguments through prompts

docs.title: Available Options
docs.text:
Bash Scripts: | Option | Short | Description | |--------|-------|-------------| | --backup | -b | Create backup before migration | | --yes | -y | Skip confirmation prompts | | --path PATH | -p PATH | Specify project path | | --help | -h | Show help message |

PowerShell Scripts: | Parameter | Description | |-----------|-------------| | -Backup | Create backup before migration | | -Yes | Skip confirmation prompts | | -Path "PATH" | Specify project path | | -Help | Show help message |

docs.title: What the Script Does
docs.text:
• Update all Floor imports to Froom imports
  • Replace FloorDatabase with FroomDatabase
  • Replace $Floor prefixes with $Froom
  • Update your pubspec.yaml dependencies
  • Clean old generated files

Note: The script can create automatic backups and provides interactive confirmations for safe migration.

docs.title: Manual Review Required
docs.text:
After running the automated migration, you should manually review:

  1. pubspec.yaml - Ensure correct version numbers
  2. Generated files - Delete old .g.dart files and regenerate
  3. Custom code - Check any custom Floor-specific code that might need updates
  4. Tests - Update any tests that reference Floor classes

docs.title: Key Differences
docs.text:
While Froom maintains API compatibility with Floor, there are some key improvements:

  1. Better analyzer support - Compatible with analyzer 11.x
  2. Modern dependencies - Updated to work with latest Flutter versions
  3. Improved error handling - Better debugging experience
  4. Active maintenance - Regular updates and bug fixes
  5. Upsert - @upsert inserts or updates entities like Room's @Upsert, including multiple parameters and partial entities (see Upsert)
  6. Lint friendly generated code - Generated files contain // ignore_for_file: type=lint, so strict lint rule sets like very_good_analysis don't report issues in them

docs.title: Common Issues
docs.text:
1. Build errors after migration
  2. Clean and rebuild: flutter packages pub run build_runner clean && flutter packages pub run build_runner build

  3. Delete existing .g.dart files manually if needed

  4. Import errors

  5. Ensure all Floor imports are replaced with Froom imports

  6. Check that you're using the correct Froom version

  7. Database builder errors

  8. Verify all $Floor prefixes are changed to $Froom

  9. PowerShell execution policy errors (Windows)

  10. Use the batch launcher: .\scripts\run_migration.bat
  11. Or temporarily bypass: PowerShell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File ".\scripts\migrate_floor_to_froom.ps1"
  12. Or check current policy: Get-ExecutionPolicy

docs.title: Getting Help
docs.text:
If you encounter issues during migration:

  • Check GitHub Issues for known issues
  • Ask questions in GitHub Discussions
  • Review the complete Froom documentation

docs.title: Migration Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Update pubspec.yaml dependencies
  • [ ] Replace all Floor imports with Froom imports
  • [ ] Update database class to extend FroomDatabase
  • [ ] Update database builder class names
  • [ ] Run migration script (optional)
  • [ ] Clean and regenerate code
  • [ ] Test your application thoroughly
  • [ ] Update any documentation references

docs.title: Migrations
docs.text:
Whenever you are doing changes to your entities, you're required to also migrate the old data.

First, update your entity. Next, Increase the database version. Define a Migration which specifies a startVersion, an endVersion and a function that executes SQL to migrate the data. At last, use addMigrations() on the obtained database builder to add migrations. The migrations have to lead from the version of the database to the current one without gaps, e.g. 1 → 2 and 2 → 3. Like in Room, of several migrations starting at the same version, the one reaching the highest version is used, e.g. a 1 → 3 migration instead of 1 → 2 and 2 → 3. Don't forget to trigger the code generator again, to create the code for handling the new entity.

// update entity with new 'nickname' field
@Entity(tableName: 'person')
class Person {
  @PrimaryKey(autoGenerate: true)
  final int id;

  @ColumnInfo(name: 'custom_name')
  final String name;

  final String nickname;

  Person(this.id, this.name, this.nickname);
}

// bump up database version
@Database(version: 2)
abstract class AppDatabase extends FroomDatabase {
  PersonDao get personDao;
}

// create migration
final migration1to2 = Migration(1, 2, (database) async {
  await database.execute('ALTER TABLE person ADD COLUMN nickname TEXT');
});

final database = await $FroomAppDatabase
    .databaseBuilder('app_database.db')
    .addMigrations([migration1to2])
    .build();

Migrations run with foreign keys disabled, as they can't be disabled within the transaction of the migrations, which e.g. recreating a table requires. Therefore, foreign key actions like ON DELETE CASCADE don't run during migrations, so delete dependent rows explicitly. After the migrations, Froom checks that they didn't add foreign key violations with PRAGMA foreign_key_check, otherwise rolls them back together with the database version and fails opening the database, and enables foreign keys again. Violations which existed before the migrations are ignored.

docs.title: Automatic Migrations
docs.text:
Like Room's @AutoMigration, Froom can generate migrations by comparing the schemas of two versions of the database. When generating the code of a database with automatic migrations or exportSchema: true, Froom exports the schema of the current version to froom_schemas/<path of the library>/<database class>/<version>.json. Commit these files, as the automatic migrations of later versions are generated from them. Enable exportSchema: true before increasing the version for the first automatic migration, so that the schema of the version to migrate from is exported. Otherwise, generate the code of the previous version with exportSchema: true once, or migrate from it with a manual Migration. The schemas are exported to another directory when configuring it in the build.yaml of your project:

targets:
  $default:
    builders:
      froom_generator:
        options:
          schema_location: database_schemas

After increasing the version, declare an AutoMigration from the previous version to the new one. Its migration is added to the database builder automatically, unless a migration of the same versions is added with addMigrations().

@Database(
  version: 2,
  entities: [Person, Song],
  autoMigrations: [AutoMigration(from: 1, to: 2)],
)
abstract class AppDatabase extends FroomDatabase {}

Froom adds new tables and columns, renames tables, and recreates tables with other changes, e.g. to their columns, primary key, foreign keys or indices, copying their data like SQLite recommends. New NOT NULL columns require a default value, see @ColumnInfo(defaultValue: ...). Views are recreated with their new queries.

Deleted and renamed tables and columns can't be distinguished, so the code generation fails until they are declared on a spec class extending AutoMigrationSpec. Its onPostMigrate method runs within the transaction of the migration afterwards, e.g. for migrating data.

import 'package:froom/sqflite.dart' as sqflite;

@Database(
  version: 3,
  entities: [Person, Artist, Song],
  autoMigrations: [
    AutoMigration(from: 1, to: 2),
    AutoMigration(from: 2, to: 3, spec: AppAutoMigrationSpec),
  ],
)
abstract class AppDatabase extends FroomDatabase {}

@RenameTable(fromTableName: 'Singer', toTableName: 'Artist')
@RenameColumn(tableName: 'Person', fromColumnName: 'name', toColumnName: 'fullName')
@DeleteTable(tableName: 'Album')
@DeleteColumn(tableName: 'Person', columnName: 'nickname')
class AppAutoMigrationSpec extends AutoMigrationSpec {
  @override
  Future<void> onPostMigrate(sqflite.Database database) async {
    // e.g. migrate data
  }
}

Specs are created by their unnamed constructor. To pass dependencies instead, annotate the spec with @providedAutoMigrationSpec and add an instance with addAutoMigrationSpecs() of the database builder.

docs.title: Destructive Migration
docs.text:
When it's fine to lose the data of the database, e.g. for a cache or during development, call fallbackToDestructiveMigration() on the database builder. Like Room, Froom then recreates the database from scratch instead of failing when there is no migration from its version to the current one, or when the database version is higher than the current one (downgrade). All tables and views get dropped, so all data is lost. Migrations are still used whenever they cover the version change.

final database = await $FroomAppDatabase
    .databaseBuilder('app_database.db')
    .addMigrations([migration1to2])
    .addCallback(Callback(
      onDestructiveMigration: (database) {
        // e.g. re-download data
      },
    ))
    .fallbackToDestructiveMigration()
    .build();

docs.title: Naming
docs.text: The library's name derives from the following. Froom as the bottom layer of a Room which points to the analogy of the database layer being the bottom and foundation layer of most applications. Where fl also gives a pointer that the library is used in the Flutter context.

docs.title: Null Safety
docs.text: Froom infers nullability of database columns directly from entity fields, as mentioned in the Entities section. When not explicitly making a field nullable by applying ? to its type, a column cannot hold NULL. For more information regarding nulls as query results, see the Queries and Streams section.

docs.title: Platform Support
docs.text: Froom supports iOS, Android, Linux, macOS, Windows and the web. It accesses SQLite through a sqflite DatabaseFactory, which can be chosen per database.

docs.title: Default Database Factory
docs.text:
Platform Default factory Android, iOS The sqflite plugin, which uses the SQLite of the system and requires the app to depend on sqflite. Background isolates have to register it with DartPluginRegistrant.ensureInitialized() Linux, macOS, Windows databaseFactoryFfi of sqflite_common_ffi, which is based on sqlite3 Web databaseFactoryFfiWeb of sqflite_common_ffi_web, see Web

The sqflite plugin stores databases passed by name to databaseBuilder() in the databases directory of the platform. The FFI factory stores them in .dart_tool/sqflite_common_ffi/databases of the working directory instead, which suits tests and command line apps. Apps using it should pass an absolute path, e.g. based on getApplicationSupportDirectory() of the path_provider package.

docs.title: Choosing the SQLite Library
docs.text:
With the FFI factory, sqlite3 bundles its own build of SQLite with the app by hooks, so no further dependency is needed. The library can be chosen per platform in the pubspec.yaml of the app, for example the SQLite of the operating system on macOS:

hooks:
  user_defines:
    sqlite3:
      source:
        macos: system
        default: sqlite3 # the bundled build

Other sources are sqlite3mc (SQLite3MultipleCiphers) and sqlcipher for encrypted databases, and custom builds of SQLite. See the hook options of sqlite3 for all of them.

Android doesn't allow apps to load the SQLite of the system with FFI, use the sqflite plugin for it instead.

As sqlite3 bundles SQLite on Android and iOS as well, apps only using the sqflite plugin there can avoid bundling it by choosing the system SQLite for these platforms, which is never loaded then:

hooks:
  user_defines:
    sqlite3:
      source:
        android: system
        ios: system
        default: sqlite3

FTS3 and FTS4

The SQLite builds bundled by sqlite3, including the encrypted ones, only support FTS5, so opening databases with entities annotated with @Fts3 or @Fts4 fails with a MissingSqliteModuleException. Use @Fts5 instead, the SQLite of the system (source: system, or the sqflite plugin on Android and iOS), or a custom build enabling SQLITE_ENABLE_FTS3.

docs.title: Choosing the Database Factory
docs.text:
Pass another factory to the builder of the database to open it with, for example the FFI one on Android and iOS, to use the bundled or an encrypted SQLite there:

import 'package:sqflite_common_ffi/sqflite_ffi.dart';

final database = await $FroomAppDatabase
    .databaseBuilder(path)
    .databaseFactory(databaseFactoryFfi)
    .build();

Any DatabaseFactory works, e.g. databaseFactoryFfiNoIsolate to run the queries on the current isolate, or the factory of another SQLite library.

Changes are only reported to the streams of the database opened by the builder, not to other isolates, processes or browser tabs writing to the same database.

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text:
Databases are encrypted with a password passed to their builder, which requires an encrypted build of SQLite like SQLite3MultipleCiphers or SQLCipher, and thus the FFI factory:

hooks:
  user_defines:
    sqlite3:
      source: sqlite3mc # or sqlcipher

final database = await $FroomAppDatabase
    .databaseBuilder(path)
    .password(password)
    .build();

Opening the database fails with a DatabaseEncryptionException if the password is wrong, the database isn't encrypted, or SQLite doesn't support encryption, e.g. the system SQLite of the sqflite plugin, instead of storing the database unencrypted. Existing unencrypted databases aren't encrypted by adding a password, which fails as well, so their data has to be copied into a new database with the password. In-memory databases aren't stored and thus not encrypted. Encryption isn't supported on the web, as the storage of sqflite_common_ffi_web doesn't support it.

docs.title: Web
docs.text:
On the web, the databases are stored in IndexedDB by sqflite_common_ffi_web, which runs SQLite compiled to WebAssembly in a shared worker. Its files have to be added to the web directory of the app once, and again after upgrading sqflite_common_ffi_web:

dart run sqflite_common_ffi_web:setup

This adds sqlite3.wasm and the worker sqflite_sw.js. Apps can be compiled both to JavaScript and to WebAssembly (flutter build web --wasm).

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Simply instantiate an in-memory database and run the database tests on your local development machine as shown in the following snippet. For more test references, check out the project's tests. They test the pure Dart package froom_common with package:test; in a Flutter project, import package:froom/froom.dart and use flutter_test as shown below.

Tests on the development machine use the FFI database factory, whose SQLite is bundled automatically, so they run without further setup. Entities annotated with @Fts3 or @Fts4 require the SQLite of the system, see Platform Support, which has to be installed on Linux, e.g. with sudo apt-get install libsqlite3-dev.

import 'package:froom/froom.dart';
import 'package:flutter_test/flutter_test.dart';

// your imports follow here
import 'dao/person_dao.dart';
import 'database.dart';
import 'model/person.dart';

void main() {
  group('database tests', () {
    late TestDatabase database;
    late PersonDao personDao;

    setUp(() async {
      database = await $FroomTestDatabase
          .inMemoryDatabaseBuilder()
          .build();
      personDao = database.personDao;
    });

    tearDown(() async {
      await database.close();
    });

    test('find person by id', () async {
      final person = Person(1, 'Simon');
      await personDao.insertPerson(person);

      final actual = await personDao.findPersonById(person.id);

      expect(actual, equals(person));
    });
  });
}

docs.title: Type Converters
docs.text:
Attention

This feature is still in an experimental state. Please use it with caution and file issues for problems you encounter.

SQLite allows storing values of only a handful types. Whenever more complex Dart in-memory objects should be stored, there sometimes is the need for converting between Dart and SQLite compatible types. Dart's DateTime, for instance, provides an object-oriented API for handling time. Objects of this class can simply be represented as int values by mapping DateTime to its timestamp in milliseconds. Instead of manually mapping between these types repeatedly, when reading and writing, type converters can be used. It's sufficient to define the conversion from a database to an in-memory type and vice versa once, which then is reused automatically.

The implementation and usage of the mentioned DateTime to int converter is described in the following.

  1. Create a converter class that extends or implements the abstract TypeConverter and supply the in-memory object type and database type as parameterized types. This class inherits the decode() and encode() functions which define the conversion from one to the other type. Implementing TypeConverter allows a class to be a converter of other libraries as well, e.g. a JsonConverter of json_annotation. 

    class DateTimeConverter extends TypeConverter<DateTime, int> {
  @override
  DateTime decode(int databaseValue) {
    return DateTime.fromMillisecondsSinceEpoch(databaseValue);
  }

  @override
  int encode(DateTime value) {
    return value.millisecondsSinceEpoch;
  }
}

  2. Apply the created type converter to the database by using the @TypeConverters annotation and make sure to additionally import the file of your type converter here. Importing it in your database file is always necessary because the generated code will be part of your database file and this is the location where your type converters get instantiated. 

    @TypeConverters([DateTimeConverter])
@Database(version: 1, entities: [Order])
abstract class OrderDatabase extends FroomDatabase {
  OrderDao get orderDao;
}

  3. Use the non-default DateTime type in an entity. 

    @entity
class Order {
  @primaryKey
  final int id;

  final DateTime date;

  Order(this.id, this.date);
}

A converter of a non-nullable type also converts the nullable type, e.g. DateTime? fields, parameters and query results. null values are stored as NULL without invoking the converter. A converter of the nullable type, e.g. TypeConverter<DateTime?, int?>, is preferred if there is one.

Type converters can be applied to

  1. databases
  2. DAOs
  3. entities/views
  4. entity/view fields
  5. DAO methods
  6. DAO method parameters

The type converter is added to the scope of the element so if you put it on a class, all methods/fields in that class will be able to use the converter.

The closest type converter wins! If you, for example, add a converter on the database level and another one on a DAO method parameter, which takes care of converting the same types, the one declared next to the DAO method parameter will be used. Please refer to the above list to get more information about the precedence of converters.
